column2: Sea ice acts as a buffer between the ocean and the ice shelves.
When sea ice is present, it dampens wave energy and reduces direct contact between warm ocean waters and ice shelf fronts.
Retreat or thinning of sea ice allows more ocean swells and warmer water to reach ice shelves, increasing the risk of:
Basal melt (melting from below)
Calving (breaking off of large ice chunks)
Sea ice retreat alters surface freshwater input and salinity, which can affect ocean stratification and circulation.
Changes in circulation can bring warm Circumpolar Deep Water (CDW) onto the continental shelf and into ice shelf cavities, accelerating basal melt.
Increased ice shelf melting adds freshwater to the ocean, reducing local salinity.
Lower salinity may inhibit sea ice formation, leading to further sea ice retreat, completing a positive feedback loop that enhances both sea ice loss and shelf melt.
Effects vary regionally and seasonally:
West Antarctic Ice Sheet and Amundsen Sea: Particularly sensitive to CDW intrusion due to reduced sea ice.
East Antarctica: Generally more stable but also vulnerable in places like the Totten Glacier region.

Modeling studies confirm that declining sea ice leads to increased ocean heat transport, undermining the stability of ice shelves.
